The One Best Way

A history of management, told through the people who invented it.

Order a latte in Hartford, in Seattle, in Tokyo. Different continent, different barista, same drink, same steps, in nearly the same number of seconds. Nothing about that is an accident. Somebody decided there was a best way to make your coffee, wrote it down, and trained the world to follow it.

This unit is about the people who invented that idea, and the people who discovered what it misses. You will meet a machinist with a stopwatch, an executive who saved a dying company with a to-do list, and a lighting experiment that refused to behave, and by the end you will see all three of them hiding inside every shift you have ever worked.

How this works

One idea per page. Read at your own pace and use Next and Back to move around.

At each checkpoint question, choose an answer and read the feedback. Wrong answers are part of the learning, so try again freely. The page unlocks when you find the right one.

Some pages are experiments you run yourself. Instead of reading about a concept, you will move a slider or make a choice and watch what changes. Those pages unlock once you have tried them.

Prefer to listen? Press the 🔊 Listen button at the top of any page and your device will read the page aloud. Press it again to stop.

There is no score and no timer. This unit is for learning, not testing.

Part 1 · The Question

Start with your own coffee

Think about the last drink you ordered at a Starbucks. Between the moment you paid and the moment your name was called, a dozen tiny decisions fired off perfectly: who took your order, who steamed the milk, how many pumps of syrup, which cup, which line you stood in.

Here is the question this unit answers: who figured all of this out? Who decided work should be measured, divided, standardized, and supervised, and who discovered that workers are not machines while doing it?

The answer is a 150-year argument, and it is genuinely a good story. But first, four words you need, because every thinker in this unit is obsessed with at least one of them.

Part 1 · The Question

Two questions, not two labels

Managers grade every decision with two words, effective and efficient. Here is a secret: you do not need to memorize which is which. Underneath the labels live two questions you already ask every day.

Question 1 · did it reach the GOAL?

Did the thing actually do what it was supposed to do? If yes, it was effective.

The word carries its own reminder: an effective action produces the effect you wanted.

Question 2 · how much did it WASTE?

Time, money, effort, milk. The less you burned getting there, the more efficient it was.

You already use this one: a car's fuel efficiency is how far it goes on the gas it burns.

GOAL is one question. WASTE is a completely separate question. A café can reach its GOAL while burning money, and it can save beautifully on milk while the line stays twenty minutes long. That is why good managers always ask both, separately, every time.

Enough definitions. The next page is just stories.

Part 1 · The Question

🧪 Experiment 1 · Five quick stories

Ask the two questions

Five little stories, one at a time. For each one, answer the same two questions. That is the whole exercise. The labels will quietly name themselves.

Story 1 of 5

☕ A café sets a GOAL: get morning waits under three minutes. A new mobile-order flow gets it done, and the store needs fewer staff-hours than before.

Did it reach the GOAL?
Did it WASTE a lot?
Reached the GOAL, wasted almost nothing. The dream combo.(A manager would call this both effective and efficient. But you just said it better.)

📚 Your GOAL: pass tomorrow’s ten-question quiz. You pull an all-nighter and reread the entire 400-page textbook. You pass, on four hours of sleep, after nine hours of studying for ten questions.

Did it reach the GOAL?
Did it WASTE a lot?
It worked… at a brutal price. GOAL reached, mountains of WASTE.(Effective, but not efficient. Also: please sleep.)

🍽 A restaurant’s GOAL: fix painfully slow desserts. The owner buys a clever gadget that chops onions in half the time. Prep costs drop nicely… and desserts come out exactly as slow as before.

Did it reach the GOAL?
Did it WASTE a lot?
Tidy, cheap, and beside the point: the GOAL never moved.(Efficient, but not effective. Fast onions were never the problem.)

🚗 Your GOAL: reach your cousin’s wedding by 3 PM. You improvise a “shortcut,” get lost, burn half a tank circling the same roundabout, and walk in after the vows.

Did it reach the GOAL?
Did it WASTE a lot?
Missed the GOAL and burned the gas.(Neither effective nor efficient. The family will retell this story forever.)

☕ A café’s GOAL: raise customer satisfaction. A new barista training program works, scores climb. It also ran triple its budget and took twice as long as planned.

Did it reach the GOAL?
Did it WASTE a lot?
GOAL reached, budget torched.(Effective, not efficient. Keep this exact story in mind: it comes back at the next checkpoint.)
What you just did

Five different stories, the same two questions every time. That pair of questions IS the concept. If you can ask did it reach the GOAL? and how much did it WASTE?, you understand effectiveness and efficiency better than someone who only memorized the definitions.

Part 1 · The Question

Productivity, and thinking in systems

Productivity

Output per unit of input. Related to efficiency, but focused on the volume produced rather than just the waste avoided.

If a barista goes from making 15 drinks an hour to 20, thanks to a faster machine, a simpler ordering app, or a smarter store layout, productivity just rose by a third. Same barista, same hour, more output.

Systematic approach

Solving problems with a structured, step-by-step method based on evidence, instead of guesswork and hunches.

Say the morning rush is producing painful lines. A systematic manager does not randomly try things. She works the steps:

Collect data. Peak times, order types, prep times, customer complaints.

Identify possible fixes. More staff at peak? A faster register system?

Test the best one small. Pilot it in one or two stores.

Measure the result. Did waits actually shrink?

Roll out what works. Expand the fix to every store.

Hold onto that word, systematic. In 1878, a young machinist is about to apply it to something nobody had ever measured before: the worker.

Part 1 · The Question

Checkpoint 1

Worked, but at what cost?

Sound familiar? A café launches a barista training program to raise customer satisfaction. Scores rise, so the GOAL is reached, but the program ran far over budget and schedule. What is the best description?

Not quite. Reread the story: satisfaction scores rose, so the GOAL was reached. The trouble is on the WASTE side.
Correct. ✓ GOAL reached: effective. Time and money torched: not efficient. Notice what you just did: you answered with the two questions, and the labels followed on their own.
Not quite. Triple the budget and double the timeline is a lot of WASTE. Only one of the two questions comes back happy.
Not quite. Scores rose, which is exactly the GOAL the program was built for. One of the two questions comes back happy.

Part 2 · Before Managers

1770: a world without managers

Picture a shoemaker's workshop before the Industrial Revolution. One craftsman makes the entire shoe: cuts the leather, shapes it, stitches it, nails the heel. He learned the trade over seven years as an apprentice. He works at his own pace and makes a few pairs a day, each one slightly different, each one his.

One person, the whole product, a few pairs a day.

Notice who is missing from this picture: a manager. There is nothing to manage. No shifts to schedule, no departments to coordinate, no production line to balance. The knowledge lives in one head and the work fits in one room.

Then, within a single lifetime, machines arrived, and that world ended.

Part 2 · Before Managers

🧪 Experiment 2 · Adam Smith's pin factory, 1776

Run the most famous experiment in economics

In 1776, the economist Adam Smith visited a pin factory and described what he saw in the opening pages of The Wealth of Nations. Making a pin involves about 18 separate operations: drawing the wire, straightening it, cutting it, sharpening the point, grinding the head, attaching it, whitening it, packaging it.

You have ten workers. Try organizing them both ways and watch the day's output.

—pins per day, all ten workers combined
—pins per worker
Choose an arrangement above to run the day.
What Smith saw

Working alone, Smith wrote, a worker "could scarce, perhaps, with his utmost industry, make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty." Divided, ten workers made upwards of 48,000 pins a day. Same people, same tools. The only thing that changed was how the work was organized.

That is the founding discovery of management: organization itself is a source of productivity. But dividing work creates a brand-new problem. Somebody now has to decide who does what, keep eighteen tasks flowing in sync, and check the results. Congratulations: you just invented the need for a manager.

Part 2 · Before Managers

The factory changes everything

The Industrial Revolution scaled Smith's pin room up by a factor of a thousand. Steam power and machines pulled work out of workshops and into factories, and the numbers involved stopped fitting inside any one person's head.

10×a textile mill ran dozens of interdependent stages, spinning to weaving to dyeing
100sof workers under one roof, strangers to each other, on machine time
1000sof miles of new railroads moving materials and finished goods on schedules

Each change created a management problem nobody had ever solved before. Mass production demanded consistent quality: when every artisan had a personal style, charm; when a factory ships ten thousand identical shirts, chaos. Railroads demanded coordination across distances and timetables. Specialization demanded that hundreds of narrow tasks click together perfectly, every hour, all day.

The vacuum

And who was in charge of all this? Essentially nobody, trained in nothing. Factory foremen ruled by shouting, favoritism, and rules of thumb. Hiring was often whoever showed up at the gate. Nobody knew how long a task should take, so nobody could plan. The only large organizations humanity had practice running were armies and churches, and factories were neither.

Into that vacuum stepped three very different kinds of thinker. The first one carried a stopwatch.

Part 2 · Before Managers

Checkpoint 2

Why then?

Management theory did not exist in the craft era, then appeared urgently during the Industrial Revolution. Why?

Not quite. Backwards. Machines raised the stakes: an unmanaged factory wasted more money in a day than an unmanaged workshop could in a year.
Not quite. No such law existed. The pressure came from inside the factories, not from regulators.
Correct. ✓ One artisan making whole shoes needs no manager. Hundreds of specialized workers, dozens of production stages, machine schedules, and railroad timetables need planning, coordination, and control. New problems demanded new thinking.
Not quite. Careful. Factory workers held plenty of skill and knowledge, as the Hawthorne researchers will prove later in this unit. What changed was the structure of work, not the intelligence of workers.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

1878: the machinist who watched

Frederick Winslow Taylor, born in 1856 to a well-off Philadelphia family, was supposed to go to Harvard. Instead he became an apprentice machinist, and by 1878 he was working his way up the floor of Midvale Steel, where he would eventually rise to chief engineer.

On that floor he noticed something that offended him to his core: everyone was working slowly on purpose.

Key term

Soldiering: deliberately working below your real capacity while appearing busy.

And here is the part managers of the era missed: the workers were being perfectly rational. Everyone was paid by the day, so producing more earned you nothing. Worse, if the crew ever revealed how fast the job could really go, the bosses would simply cut the piece rate or raise the quota. Working slowly was not laziness. It was self-defense.

Taylor's radical question: nobody actually knows how long this job should take. Not the workers, not the foremen, nobody. What if, instead of guessing and shouting, we measured it?

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

The pig iron story

Taylor's most famous demonstration came at Bethlehem Steel around 1899. Laborers spent their days hauling 92-pound bars of crude iron, called pig iron, up a ramp into rail cars. The average man loaded about 12.5 tons a day.

Taylor studied the job, timed every step, and calculated that a first-class worker, given exactly prescribed rest breaks at exactly the right moments, could load nearly four times as much without harm. He selected a strong, hardworking Dutch immigrant he called "Schmidt," offered him a raise from $1.15 to $1.85 a day, and told him to do precisely as instructed: lift when told, rest when told, no decisions required.

12.5tons per day, the old average
47.5tons per day, Schmidt under Taylor's method
+61%Schmidt's raise, for 280% more output

Look at those last two numbers together, because the whole future argument over Taylorism lives in the gap between them: output nearly quadrupled, pay rose 61 percent. Who captured the difference?

A historian's footnote 🧐

Decades later, researchers dug into the records and found that Taylor polished this story: the numbers were shakier and the science messier than his book admits. Savor the irony. The father of measurement massaged his data. Treat the story as a parable of the method, and remember that even famous evidence deserves a second look.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

🧪 Experiment 3 · The science of shoveling, 1898

Find the one best shovel

Real experiment, straight from Bethlehem Steel. Workers shoveled everything from feather-light rice coal to heavy iron ore using whatever shovel they owned, so every scoop weighed something different. Taylor asked a question nobody had asked: what scoop weight moves the most material in a day?

Drag the slider. You are running his experiment: same worker, same day, different shovel load.

6 lbs · tiny scoops38 lbs · monster scoops
6 lbsper scoop
—tons moved by one worker in a day
Start sliding to run the experiment.
You found it

Taylor's answer was about 21½ pounds. Too light and you waste motions on tiny scoops; too heavy and fatigue destroys the afternoon. So Bethlehem stopped letting workers bring their own shovels and issued designed ones: a small flat scoop for heavy ore, a huge deep one for light rice coal, each landing every scoop near 21 pounds.

16→59tons handled per worker per day
+60%higher wages for shovelers on the new system
500→140workers needed in the yard

Read that third number again, though. Efficiency delivered, and 360 jobs disappeared. Both facts are true at once, and both belong in your notes.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

Scientific management, principle by principle

What you just did with the slider, Taylor did with a stopwatch, thousands of times. In 1911 he published The Principles of Scientific Management, and the method inside it has three moves you will recognize instantly from your own jobs.

1 · Time and motion studies

Observe the work, time every step, break it into motions, and eliminate the unnecessary ones, because for every task there is "one best way." At a Starbucks, that is someone analyzing exactly how a barista builds a latte and finding the wasted reach, the extra step, the backtrack to the fridge.

2 · Standardization

Once the best way is found, everyone is trained to do it that way. That is why your latte tastes the same in Hartford and Tokyo: pumps of syrup counted, milk steamed to a set temperature, steps in a set order. The recipe is not a suggestion. It is the point.

3 · Incentives

Give workers a reason to embrace the new method: link pay to output. Taylor's version, the differential piece-rate system, paid a low rate per unit below the daily standard and a high rate at or above it. Hit the standard and your whole day repriced. You will feel how sharp that is on the next page.

⏱ UPS engineers its drivers' routes and motions, down to how to hold keys 🍔 McDonald's operations manual specifies nearly everything 📦 Amazon tracks warehouse scans by the second

Taylor died in 1915. His stopwatch did not.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

🧪 Experiment 4 · The differential piece rate

Feel the incentive

You are a machinist in Taylor's shop. The scientifically set standard is 60 finished pieces a day. Below standard you earn 2¢ per piece; make standard and the rate jumps to 3¢ for every piece. The old shop next door still pays a flat $1.15 a day no matter what.

Slide your day's output and watch both paychecks.

40 piecesstandard: 6080 pieces
$1.15old shop: flat day wage, any output
—Taylor's shop: differential piece rate
Slide to see your pay.
The psychology of the jump

Did you feel it? At 59 pieces you earn $1.18. One more piece and you earn $1.80. That cliff is deliberate: it makes the standard impossible to ignore and soldiering expensive. Under day wages, effort was invisible. Under the differential rate, effort is the paycheck.

Now the caveat your textbook will echo: money turned out to be a narrower motivator than Taylor believed. Workers also feared, reasonably, that hitting high numbers would just get the standard raised. Park that suspicion. It resurfaces at a factory called Hawthorne.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

The deal underneath it all

Taylor insisted scientific management was not just stopwatches and pay tricks. His 1911 book frames it as four duties, a new deal between managers and workers:

Develop a science for each task. Replace rule-of-thumb with measured knowledge.

Scientifically select and train workers, instead of letting them pick up habits alone.

Cooperate with workers to ensure the work follows the science.

Divide the work between managers and workers: managers plan, workers execute.

Read that fourth duty again slowly, because it is the most consequential sentence in this unit so far. Taylor split thinking from doing. Planning became a full-time job belonging to a new class of people, and that is where the modern manager comes from. Every planning department, every corporate office, every "that decision is above your pay grade" traces back to this split.

Hold this thought

Taylor honestly believed both sides would win: higher wages for workers, higher output for owners, prosperity for everyone. But notice what the worker loses in his system: the right to think about the work. Schmidt was told when to lift and when to rest. The shoemaker from Part 2 had vanished completely.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

Checkpoint 3

Diagnose the shop floor

Before Taylor, workers at Midvale deliberately worked below capacity, a practice called soldiering. According to Taylor's own analysis, why did they do it?

Not quite. They could go much faster, and everyone on the floor knew it. That is what made the slowdown deliberate rather than a limitation.
Correct. ✓ Soldiering was rational self-defense inside a badly designed system. Taylor's insight was to change the system rather than blame the workers, though his fix created new problems we are about to meet.
Not quite. Soldiering happened with or without unions. It grew out of the pay system itself: when effort is invisible to the paycheck, effort quietly disappears.
Not quite. If machines had been the bottleneck, Taylor's methods could not have quadrupled output with the same equipment.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

The disciples: a bricklayer and a chart

Taylor's ideas spread through two remarkable followers you should be able to name.

Frank & Lillian Gilbreth · motion studies

Frank Gilbreth started as a bricklayer's apprentice and got obsessed with wasted movement. Filming and analyzing the job, he cut the motions in laying a brick from 18 to about 5, and a good mason's daily output roughly tripled. With his wife Lillian Gilbreth, a pioneering psychologist of work, the Gilbreths catalogued the basic units of all human motion, which they named therbligs (spell "Gilbreth" nearly backwards). Lillian outlived Frank by decades, became one of the first great women of engineering and management, and pushed the field toward the worker's wellbeing, fatigue, and morale. Remember her: she is a bridge to everything in Part 6.

Henry Gantt · make the plan visible

Taylor's colleague Henry Gantt drew work as horizontal bars on a calendar: what starts when, what depends on what, what is late. The Gantt chart helped schedule everything from factory floors to World War I shipbuilding, and it is sitting inside every project management tool you will ever use, from Microsoft Project to Asana to Monday.com, essentially unchanged after a century.

1910s technology, still running your group projects.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

The backlash

Workers, it turns out, hated being timed. To many, the stopwatch was not science. It was surveillance, speed-up, and the theft of their craft knowledge, handed to a planning office that would use it to squeeze them.

In 1911, workers at the Watertown Arsenal walked out when a time-study man started timing them. Congress hauled Taylor in for four days of hostile hearings in 1912, and later attached riders to appropriations bills that banned stopwatch studies in Army arsenals for over three decades.

The critique, in one line

Scientific management treated the worker as a well-oiled machine part, and human beings do not experience being a machine part quietly.

And Taylorism never died; it upgraded its tools. When an Amazon warehouse system tracks seconds between scans and flags "time off task," when delivery apps score every route, that is the stopwatch reborn as software. The productivity gains are real. So is the burnout and turnover that come with being measured every second, which is why this debate is still alive in the news, a century later.

Something was missing from Taylor's picture of a worker. It took a lighting experiment gone wrong to find it. But first, while Taylor was staring at tasks, a French executive was staring at something bigger.

Part 3 · The Stopwatch

Checkpoint 4

The blind spot

Scientific management transformed productivity, yet triggered strikes and Congressional hearings. What was its core blind spot?

Not quite. The output gains were real and often dramatic. The problem was never whether it worked; it was what it left out.
Not quite. The instruments were fine. Even with perfect measurements, something about the human being holding the shovel was being missed.
Correct. ✓ Motions and pay were engineered; meaning, pride, fear, and belonging were not in the model. That missing half of the human being is exactly what the next generation of researchers stumbled into.
Not quite. Pay rose far less than output did, which fueled the resentment. Generosity was not the system's failure mode.

Part 4 · The Manager's Desk

1888: the company that was supposed to die

Henri Fayol was born in 1841 in Istanbul, where his French engineer father was working on a bridge across the Golden Horn. Trained as a mining engineer, Fayol spent his entire career at one French mining and steel company, Commentry-Fourchambault, and in 1888 he was handed the top job under grim circumstances: the firm was sliding toward bankruptcy.

The view from the top: Fayol ran Commentry-Fourchambault from a desk like this for thirty years.

Fayol ran it for thirty years. No miracle invention, no lucky ore strike. He simply managed it, deliberately and well, and left it financially strong. Then he did the thing that puts him in this unit: he sat down and asked, what exactly was I doing all those years? His answer, published in 1916, became the first general theory of management.

Taylor vs. Fayol, in one glance

Taylor stood on the shop floor looking down at a single task: how should this worker shovel? Fayol sat at the director's desk looking across the whole organization: how should this company run? Bottom-up meets top-down. Modern management needs both, which is why you are learning both.

Part 4 · The Manager's Desk

The five functions: what managing actually is

Fayol's first gift was a simple, radical claim: management is not a personality or a birthright. It is a set of functions anyone can learn. Five of them:

Planning. Set goals and chart the course. A smartphone maker targets 10% more market share, then maps the ad campaigns, features, and distribution to get there.

Organizing. Arrange people, resources, and tasks into a structure: departments for product, marketing, sales, service, each with clear roles and reporting lines.

Commanding (today we say leading). Guide and motivate: the restaurant manager setting expectations, coaching the waitstaff, modeling the standard on a brutal Saturday night.

Coordinating. Keep the parts in sync: an event company aligning the venue, the speakers, the registrations, and the AV crew so one conference happens instead of four collisions.

Controlling. Monitor results against the plan and correct course: a retail chain compares each store's sales to target and intervenes where numbers sag.

Textbook bridge 📖

Your textbook compresses these into four: planning, organizing, leading, controlling, the POLC framework, with coordinating absorbed into the others. When you meet POLC, you are reading Fayol, lightly edited by a century.

Definitions are easy to nod along to. Let's see if you can spot the functions in the wild.

Part 4 · The Manager's Desk

🧪 Experiment 5 · A store manager's Monday

Tag the function

Here is one Monday in the life of Maya, who manages a busy Starbucks. Five moments, five functions, each used exactly once. Tag each moment; the day fills in as you go.

7:30 AM. Before opening, Maya sketches next week's staffing around Wednesday's new drink launch and sets a target: keep mobile-order waits under four minutes all launch week.

9:00 AM. She assigns the new hire to register, moves Jo to the espresso bar, and decides who covers each break so every station stays staffed.

11:30 AM. Mid-rush, energy is dipping. Maya jumps on bar, shows the new hire a smoother steaming technique, and rallies the team through the last hour of the rush.

1:00 PM. She calls the other shift supervisor and the bakery vendor to sync Wednesday's delivery with the launch promo, so the pastries and the new drink land together.

4:30 PM. Maya compares today's sales and milk-waste numbers against target, spots that waste is creeping up, and books a refresher on portioning for Thursday.

Fayol's point, proven

One ordinary Monday contained all five functions. That was Fayol's claim exactly: management is not mysterious charisma. It is a learnable cycle of activities, running constantly, in every organization, at every level.

Two bosses walk into a café

A barista gets told by the store manager to restock the pastry case now, while the district supervisor, visiting the store, tells her to drop everything and deep-clean the machines. She cannot do both, and both outrank her. Which of Fayol's principles is being violated?

Not quite. Division of work is about specializing tasks for efficiency. Her problem is not what her job is; it is that two authorities are pulling it in two directions.
Correct. ✓ Each employee should receive orders from one boss. The moment two chains of authority land on one person, you get confusion, stress, and conflict, exactly what Fayol designed the principle to prevent.
Not quite. Esprit de corps is team spirit and unity. Morale may well suffer here, but the structural failure is about who gives orders to whom.

Part 5 · The Rulebook

Weber: why every big organization feels the same

Ever noticed that your college's registrar, the DMV, a hospital, and a McDonald's franchise all run on the same skeleton? Forms, procedures, job titles, approval chains. That skeleton has an author.

While Taylor timed tasks and Fayol ran his company, the German sociologist Max Weber (say it VAY-ber, 1864–1920) asked the deepest question of the three: why should anyone obey a manager at all? For most of history, authority came from tradition (obey the king's son) or charisma (obey the hero). Both die with the person. Weber described a third kind, built for the industrial age: rational-legal authority, where people obey the office and its rules, not the individual holding it.

An organization built on that idea he called a bureaucracy, and he meant it as the ideal design, not the insult:

Clear division of labor, with defined jobs and the authority that goes with each.

A hierarchy where every position reports to a higher one.

Formal written rules and records, applied the same way every time.

Impersonality: decisions follow rules, not moods, friendships, or family ties.

Careers based on merit: hired and promoted for qualifications, not connections.

Before you roll your eyes

Remember what bureaucracy replaced: jobs handed to nephews, promotions by whim, one rule for the foreman's friends and another for everyone else. "Impersonal" was the reform. The same design that gives us red tape is also why your grade appeal follows a written procedure instead of depending on whether the dean likes you. Every McDonald's tastes the same because a franchise manual, pure applied Weber, makes the person behind the counter almost interchangeable with any other trained crew member on Earth.

Part 5 · The Rulebook

Checkpoint 6

Defend the paperwork

A classmate groans: "Bureaucracy is just pointless red tape." According to Weber, what was bureaucracy actually designed to achieve?

Not quite. Slowness is a side effect nobody designed in. Weber's aim pointed at a different target entirely.
Not quite. Hierarchy exists in his model, but as a way to fix accountability, not as an employment program.
Correct. ✓ Rules applied identically, records kept, careers earned by qualification: bureaucracy was the cure for nepotism and arbitrary bosses. Whether the cure has side effects, every DMV line in America can testify. But the design goal was fairness at scale.
Not quite. The exact opposite. Rational-legal authority attaches power to the office and its rules so the organization survives any individual, charismatic or not.

Part 6 · The People

1924: a routine experiment in Cicero, Illinois

Just outside Chicago stood the Hawthorne Works of Western Electric, the factory that built America's telephones. It was a city in itself: tens of thousands of workers, its own hospital, its own fire brigade.

In 1924, engineers there launched the most Taylor-style study imaginable. The question was pure scientific management: does better lighting make workers more productive? Simple. Measurable. What could go wrong?

The Hawthorne Works, Cicero, Illinois. Keep your eye on the lamps.

The engineers split workers into groups, adjusted the lights, and tracked output. On the next page, you are the engineer. Run the study and see what they saw.

Part 6 · The People

🧪 Experiment 6 · The illumination studies

Adjust the lights. Explain the output.

You are running the test room. Change the lighting however you like, several times, and watch the output line. Try turning it up. Then try turning it down. Trust your instruments.

5 / 10lighting level in the test room
100output · relays assembled (index)
The room hums along at baseline. Make your first change.
Look at your data 🤨

Brighter: output rose. Dimmer: output rose again. In the real studies, output held up even when researchers dimmed the room to roughly moonlight, and here is the detail that broke everyone's brain: the control group, whose lighting never changed at all, improved too.

The lights were never the variable that mattered. The workers knew they were part of an experiment. Someone was paying attention to them, asking their opinions, treating them as interesting. So they worked better, whatever the wattage. The most important discovery in the history of management was an accident.

Part 6 · The People

Naming the accident

Key term

The Hawthorne effect: people change their behavior, usually for the better, when they know they are being observed and feel their work matters.

Western Electric kept pulling the thread. In the relay assembly test room (1927), five women assembling telephone relays were moved to a separate room where researchers varied rest breaks, hours, and snacks. Output climbed almost no matter what they changed, rising about 30% over the studies, and stayed high even when the perks were taken away.

Why? Interviewed, the women were clear. In the test room they were consulted before changes, nobody hovered over them, and the five of them had become a team that liked being together. A supervisor listened instead of policing. They mattered, so they worked.

The experiments ran until 1932, and in 1928 the company brought in a Harvard researcher to explain results that refused to behave: Elton Mayo. His interpretation launched a movement.

The human relations movement

The school of thought, roughly the 1930s through the 1960s, holding that social and psychological factors, belonging, attention, group dynamics, satisfaction, drive productivity as much as physical conditions and pay.

Part 6 · The People

What Mayo concluded, and where it lives now

Mayo's message to managers was a direct inversion of Taylor: your workers are not machine parts that respond to pay and lighting. Work is a social activity. The informal group, the friendships, the sense of being valued, these move the numbers as much as any stopwatch ever did. Two of his descendants are words you will hear in every modern workplace:

Employee engagement

The emotional commitment employees have to their work, colleagues, and organization.

Social cohesion

The sense of unity, trust, and teamwork within a group.

Watch it work at Starbucks: partners (Starbucks deliberately does not say "employees") get health benefits and tuition covered even part-time, input on drink launches and store issues, recognition rituals, team events. Engaged partners go the extra mile with customers, and cohesive teams survive brutal rushes with their humor intact. That is Mayo's playbook, run at global scale.

The modern proof 🔬

Decades later, Google ran Project Aristotle, crunching data on hundreds of its own teams to find what makes teams effective. The answer was not star talent, perks, or even who was on the team. The top factor was psychological safety: members feel safe to speak up, ask, admit mistakes. A century of tools later, the data landed exactly where Mayo did: how people feel in the group drives how the group performs.

Part 6 · The People

The honest footnotes

Two footnotes keep this story honest, and both make you smarter about managing.

Footnote 1 · the group can also slow things down

In the bank wiring observation room (1931), Hawthorne researchers watched 14 men wiring switchboards. The group had quietly set its own idea of a fair day's work, below what the company's incentive plan pushed for, and enforced it. Work too fast and you were a "rate buster"; too slow, a "chiseler." Either way the group brought you back in line with mockery and the occasional punch on the arm. Group norms are powerful, and they do not automatically point in management's direction. Any incentive plan that ignores the group, like Taylor's, is in for a surprise.

Footnote 2 · the science was messy

Later scholars re-examined the Hawthorne data and found the studies were loosely designed by modern standards: tiny samples, changed conditions, replaced participants. Like Taylor's pig iron tale, the legend outgrew the evidence. Yet the core insight has been confirmed so many times since, from engagement research to Project Aristotle, that the conclusion outlived the imperfect experiment that revealed it.

Part 6 · The People

Checkpoint 7

The real variable

In the Hawthorne studies, output rose when lighting improved, rose when lighting was dimmed, and rose in the control group whose lighting never changed. What was actually driving productivity?

Not quite. Adaptation cannot explain the control group improving with no change at all, and it says nothing about why output climbed when breaks and hours changed too.
Correct. ✓ The experiment itself was the treatment. Feeling seen, consulted, and bonded to a team moved output more than any physical variable, which is the Hawthorne effect, and the founding evidence of the human relations movement.
Not quite. Pay arrangements barely changed across most conditions, and output stayed high even when perks were removed. Money alone cannot explain the pattern, which is precisely why the study rattled Taylor's assumptions.
Not quite. The pattern repeated across rooms, years, and conditions, and interviews with the workers themselves pointed to the same explanation: someone was finally paying attention.

✓ Unlocked. Hit Next to keep going.

Part 6 · The People

The prophet nobody listened to

Here is the unfair part of this chapter: much of what Mayo's movement "discovered" in the 1930s, a Boston woman had already written down years earlier, to polite applause and little action.

Mary Parker Follett (1868–1933) came to management sideways: educated at Radcliffe when women could not get Harvard degrees, then decades running community centers in Boston's immigrant neighborhoods, watching how real groups actually make decisions. By the 1920s, executives were quietly attending her lectures, and she was saying things almost nobody in business was ready to hear:

Real leadership means power with people, not power over them. Mary Parker Follett's central idea, in her own terms

Managers, she argued, should be facilitators who harness the knowledge of the people doing the work: involve employees in decisions, let authority follow expertise rather than rank, and treat conflict not as a fire to stamp out but as a signal carrying information, energy that can produce something better than either side's starting position.

She died in 1933, before the human relations movement took off, and American business largely forgot her for decades while her ideas quietly shaped thinkers abroad, especially in Japan. When management guru Peter Drucker rediscovered her work, he called her "the prophet of management." Everything from participative management to modern conflict resolution has her fingerprints on it. Time to try her most famous idea yourself.

Part 6 · The People

🧪 Experiment 7 · Follett's window, 1925

Resolve one small war

Follett's own example, from a Harvard library reading room. Two people, one window. One wants it open. One wants it closed. A tiny conflict with the exact anatomy of a big one. You are the third person in the room: try each of Follett's three ways of resolving conflict and watch what each one leaves behind. Try all three.

Pick an approach to see how it plays out.
Follett's point

Domination and compromise fight over positions (window open vs. window shut). Integration digs for interests: one person wanted fresh air, the other wanted no draft blowing on her. Nobody actually needed that window. Open the window in the empty room next door and both people get everything they wanted.

Integration is not always available, Follett admitted, but it is almost never even looked for. Sixty years later, the famous negotiation method in Getting to Yes, interests over positions, was teaching the world what she wrote in 1925.

✓ Unlocked. Hit Next to keep going.

Part 6 · The People

Checkpoint 8

Integration or compromise?

Two Starbucks shift supervisors clash over the one Saturday closer slot: both want it for the extra hours. The store manager digs into why: one wants more total hours for tuition money; the other specifically wants Saturday to avoid a weekday childcare gap. She gives Saturday to the second, and builds the first a schedule with more total hours across the week. Both walk away fully satisfied. What did the manager just do?

Not quite. Check the ending: neither supervisor gave up what they actually needed. Meeting in the middle would look like splitting the Saturdays and leaving both half-satisfied.
Not quite. She did decide, but the solution came from the supervisors' own underlying needs, not from overriding them. Domination wins the argument and loses the loser.
Correct. ✓ Positions said "I want Saturday." Interests said "I need hours" and "I need childcare-friendly timing," and those two interests never actually conflicted. That is Follett's integration: the conflict was carrying information about a better schedule.
Not quite. The Hawthorne effect is about behavior changing under observation. This scenario is about resolving a conflict by digging beneath positions to interests.

✓ Unlocked. Hit Next to keep going.

Part 7 · The Toolbox

Layers, not eras

Here is the mistake students make with this history: assuming each school replaced the one before, the way phones replace phones. Wrong. Nothing was replaced. Every school is still running, simultaneously, in every well-managed company you walk into.

Walk into a Starbucks and look for the layers. The drink recipes and steaming temperatures: Taylor. The store manager planning, organizing, leading, controlling: Fayol. The franchise-grade operations manual and HR procedures that work identically in every store: Weber. Calling workers "partners," tuition benefits, team culture, asking baristas for input: Mayo and Follett. One café, five dead theorists, all on shift.

Part 7 · The Toolbox

🧪 Experiment 8 · The capstone

Your café is struggling. Choose your lens.

The situation: you manage a café. Afternoon shifts have gone flat: drinks are coming out slow and inconsistent, two baristas are feuding about who restocks, and the newest hire looks lost nobody trained her properly. Head office wants it fixed by Friday.

You know three schools of thought. Put on each lens and see what it notices, what it fixes, and what it misses. Try all three.

Pick a lens to diagnose the shift.
The punchline of the whole unit

Which lens was right? All of them saw something real, and none saw everything. The slow drinks are partly a standards problem (Taylor), partly a structure problem (Fayol), and the feud is a people problem carrying information (Follett). A real manager stacks the lenses.

Management eventually gave your instinct a formal name: the contingency approach. There is no one best way to manage; the right tool depends on the situation. Yes, the field spent fifty years hunting for the one best way, then concluded it does not exist. The unit's title was a trap. Sorry. 😌

✓ Unlocked. Hit Next to keep going.

Part 7 · The Toolbox

What came after (a fast-forward)

Your course will meet these later, so here is the trailer for everything downstream of our story:

The quantitative school (1940s+). World War II taught the military to optimize convoys and logistics with math, and business borrowed it. Every UPS route optimization and airline pricing model is this school at work. Taylor's measuring instinct, upgraded to algorithms.

Systems thinking (1950s+). The organization as a living organism: inputs, transformation, outputs, feedback. Change one part, the whole shifts, so no department can be understood alone.

The contingency approach (1960s+). The punchline you just discovered, formalized: effective management depends on the situation, the technology, the environment, and the people.

The quality movement (1950s–80s). W. Edwards Deming, ignored in America, rebuilt Japanese industry around quality and worker involvement. Toyota's system lets any worker stop the entire line when they spot a defect: Taylor's standardization fused with genuine respect for worker judgment. The two rivals of our story, finally married.

Today: evidence-based management. People analytics, engagement surveys, A/B-tested policies. Hawthorne's instinct with better statistics, and the same old risk: measure the human out of the human being, and you rediscover 1911 the hard way.

Part 7 · The Toolbox

Checkpoint 9 · The last one

Name that ghost

An Amazon warehouse tracks the seconds between each worker's scans and flags anyone whose pace drops. A century earlier, whose method is this the direct descendant of, and what would the Hawthorne researchers predict about it?

Not quite. Fayol worked at the level of the whole organization: functions, structures, principles. Timing individual task motions is a different toolbox.
Correct. ✓ Second-by-second task measurement is time study reborn as software, and the Hawthorne lesson says treating people as measured parts eventually surfaces as burnout, turnover, and resistance. You now own both halves of that analysis, which is the whole point of this unit.
Not quite. Weber is about rules, hierarchy, and impersonal fairness in how the organization runs, not about timing physical tasks.
Not quite. Follett's power-with philosophy is close to the opposite of surveillance-driven pacing. She belongs to the critique of this system, not its ancestry.

Cheat Sheet

The whole cast, one line each

Screenshot this page. No memorizing required, just a place to look things up.

The people

Adam Smith (1776) · Division of labor. Ten pin-makers, work divided: 48,000 pins instead of 200.

Frederick Taylor (1856–1915) · Scientific management: time and motion studies, standardization, the "one best way," differential piece-rate pay. The Principles of Scientific Management, 1911.

Frank & Lillian Gilbreth · Motion studies (bricklaying, 18 motions to about 5); therbligs. Lillian: psychology of work, "First Lady of Management."

Henry Gantt · The Gantt chart, still inside every project management tool.

Henri Fayol (1841–1925) · Administrative management: the five functions (plan, organize, command, coordinate, control) and 14 principles. Saved Commentry-Fourchambault, wrote it down in 1916.

Max Weber (1864–1920) · Bureaucracy: rational-legal authority, hierarchy, formal rules, impersonality, merit careers. Fairness at scale, red tape as the side effect.

Elton Mayo (1880–1949) · Interpreter of the Hawthorne studies (1924–1932): work is social; attention and group life drive output. Human relations movement.

Mary Parker Follett (1868–1933) · Power with, not power over; constructive conflict; integration. Ahead of the movement she inspired. Drucker's "prophet of management."

Key terms in one line each

Efficiency · the WASTE question: how much time, money, and effort did it burn? Doing things right.

Effectiveness · the GOAL question: did it do what it was supposed to do? Doing the right things.

Productivity · output per unit of input.

Soldiering · deliberately working below capacity; rational under badly designed pay.

Time and motion study · measure a task's steps to find and cut wasted effort.

Standardization · everyone trained to the one best method found.

Differential piece rate · low rate below the standard, high rate at or above it: the pay cliff.

Unity of command · one employee, one boss (Fayol's most-quoted principle).

Esprit de corps · team spirit as a management responsibility.

Bureaucracy · Weber's rule-based, impersonal, merit-driven organization design.

Hawthorne effect · people improve when observed and made to feel they matter.

Employee engagement · emotional commitment to work and organization.

Social cohesion · unity, trust, and teamwork within a group.

Integration · Follett's conflict resolution: satisfy the underlying interests of both sides, so nobody loses.

Contingency approach · there is no one best way; the right method depends on the situation.

Finish

You made it through ⏱️

Nine checkpoints, eight experiments, and one big idea: every theory in this unit is a reaction to the one before it, and every one of them is still on shift at your job.

The whole unit in eight lines
  1. Two questions grade every decision: did it reach the GOAL (that is effectiveness), and how much did it WASTE (that is efficiency)? Ask both.
  2. Dividing labor (Smith's pin factory) creates massive productivity, and creates the manager.
  3. Taylor: measure the work, standardize the best way, tie pay to output. It works, and it costs something human.
  4. Workers answered the stopwatch with strikes, and Congress listened: efficiency without dignity does not stay quiet.
  5. Fayol: management is five learnable functions and 14 flexible principles, seen from the top of a company he saved.
  6. Weber: bureaucracy was designed for fairness at scale; the red tape came free.
  7. Hawthorne: workers improved whatever the lights did, because someone finally paid attention. Work is social.
  8. Follett: power with, not power over, and inside every conflict, information. There is no one best way: it depends.
Reflection · bring it with you

Think of a job you have actually worked (or your life as a student, which is also a job). Find one trace of Taylor (something timed, scripted, or standardized) and one trace of Mayo or Follett (something built to make you feel seen, included, or heard). Which of the two did your workplace do better, and what did that feel like from the inside? Two or three sentences, in your notes. We will build on this all term.
